claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin native oxide film.
The stability and adherence of the native iron-oxide scale control whether Q235 steel degrades or remains protected in both room-temperature and 700–900 °C salt environments.
An adherent magnetite/spinel scale that survives thermal transformation and spallation buffers corrosive attack.
High temperature can transform the protective scale into less-protective hematite or cause it to detach.
At room temperature, the native Q235 oxide is primarily magnetite or mixed iron oxide and remains adherent and protective in the selected salt.
At 700–900 °C, phase transitions or differential thermal expansion can destabilize the oxide scale.
Scale transformation or spallation exposes the iron substrate and accelerates corrosive attack.
Accelerated salt attack can produce measurable mass change and near-surface microstructural or compositional degradation.
Relative to room-temperature exposure, high-temperature Q235 exposure will show a significantly different mass change together with oxide transformation or spallation.
Mass loss would indicate substrate attack, whereas anomalous mass gain could result from poorly adherent corrosion products.
If the oxide remains stable at high temperature, Q235 steel will experience minimal additional degradation.
If the oxide is destabilized at high temperature, the corrosion rate will be markedly higher.
Room-temperature Q235 specimens retain an intact native oxide that ensures limited corrosion and therefore provide an appropriate reference.
The proposed mechanism applies under oxidizing salt conditions that support formation and transformation of an iron-oxide scale.
The mechanism may not apply when oxide formation is insignificant or when nonthermal mechanical stresses dominate failure.
Mass change measurements and EDS cross-sectional analysis can reveal salt-corrosion mass loss, elemental dissolution, and attack depth.
The overall role of oxide-scale stability in high-temperature corrosion is well recognized by similar studies.
The oxide phase composition, transformation temperature, and adhesion behavior of Q235 in the proposed salt remain undetermined.
An unchanged, adherent high-temperature oxide accompanied by no additional mass change would falsify the proposed oxide-stability mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome explicitly states that a stable high-temperature oxide should produce minimal additional degradation, but the falsification rule treats an unchanged adherent oxide with no additional mass change as falsifying. That observation is consistent with the hypothesis's protection branch rather than decisive falsification.
